title: Retaining Franchise Talent Presumes You Know Who They Are
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that every organization depends on a small core of "franchise players" whose departure would be genuinely destabilizing, and that leaders often fail to name them explicitly. It distinguishes different types of indispensable talent, from deep technical expertise to relationship-holders and process experts. The author notes that even large organizations rarely have more than about 25 such people. The piece calls on leaders to move beyond a vague sense of who matters most and build a specific, deliberate list, then invest personal attention in those relationships regardless of hierarchy level.
points: Every organization has a small set of "franchise players" who would seriously hurt the organization if they all left at once.
Franchise talent varies in kind: technical specialists, relationship-holders with key stakeholders, and those who understand how the organization actually works.
Even in large organizations, the number of true franchise players is rarely more than about 25.
Leaders should identify these people by name rather than relying on a general sense of who is important.
Retention requires senior leaders to build direct relationships with franchise players even when they sit several levels below them.
quotes: In any organization, a small group of contributors makes an oversized difference in getting things done and achieving results.
Even in large organizations, the number of franchise players is rarely more than 25.
Good leaders know exactly who the franchise players are. They think about them often and do everything in their power to keep them engaged and satisfied.
Retaining the franchise players is among the most important facets of great leadership.
No need to label or tell these team members how priceless they are. The key is to show them.
